sectionTitle: Use of amount of substance in relation to masses of pure substances

specStatements.text: Chemical amounts are measured in moles. The symbol for the unit mole is mol.
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass.
One mole of a substance contains the same number of the stated particles, atoms, molecules or ions as one mole of any other substance.
The number of atoms, molecules or ions in a mole of a given substance is the Avogadro constant. The value of the Avogadro constant is 6.02 x 10²³ per mole.

Students should understand that the measurement of amounts in moles can apply to atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, formulae and equations, for example that in one mole of carbon (C) the number of atoms is the same as the number of molecules in one mole of carbon dioxide (CO₂ ).
Students should be able to use the relative formula mass of a substance to calculate the number of moles in a given mass of that substance and vice versa.
The masses of reactants and products can be calculated from balanced symbol equations.
Chemical equations can be interpreted in terms of moles. For example:
Mg +2HCI →MgCI₂+ H₂
shows that one mole of magnesium reacts with two moles of hydrochloric acid to produce one mole of magnesium chloride and one mole of hydrogen gas.
Students should be able to:
calculate the masses of substances shown in a balanced symbol equation
calculate the masses of reactants and products from the balanced symbol equation and the mass of a given reactant or product.

The balancing numbers in a symbol equation can be calculated from the masses of reactants and products by converting the masses in grams to amounts in moles and converting the numbers of moles to simple whole number ratios.
Students should be able to balance an equation given the masses of reactants and products.
Students should be able to change the subject of a mathematical equation.

In a chemical reaction involving two reactants, it is common to use an excess of one of the reactants to ensure that all of the other reactant is used. The reactant that is completely used up is called the limiting reactant because it limits the amount of products.
Students should be able to explain the effect of a limiting quantity of a reactant on the amount of products it is possible to obtain in terms of amounts in moles or masses in grams.
Many chemical reactions take place in solutions. The concentration of a solution can be measured in mass per given volume of solution, eg grams per dm³ (g/dm³ ).
Students should be able to:
calculate the mass of solute in a given volume of solution of known concentration in terms of mass per given volume of solution
(HT only) explain how the mass of a solute and the volume of a solution is related to the concentration of the solution.

scopeNotes.statement: Many chemical reactions take place in solutions. The concentration of a solution can be measured in mass per given volume of solution, eg grams per dm³ (g/dm³ ).
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Concentration is treated in this section only as mass per given volume of solution, in g/dm³, which is the only measure the statement names. Nothing here introduces concentration in mol/dm³, which belongs to 4.8.3, and no item asks students to convert between the two or to use concentration in a titration calculation. Every concentration question gives or asks for a mass of solute and a volume of solution, and volumes are always converted to dm³ before use so that the unit the statement gives is the unit that is actually applied.

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) explain how the mass of a solute and the volume of a solution is related to the concentration of the solution.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The two items that ask students to explain how mass of solute and volume of solution set the concentration (q22 and q23), the concept c23 and the misconceptions m20 and m21 are all tiered higher, matching the (HT only) marking on this statement. The remaining concentration material - what concentration is, its unit, and calculating the mass of solute in a given volume - is tiered both, so a Foundation student meets only what 4.3.2.5 asks of them and is never assessed on the explanation reserved for Higher tier.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to use the relative formula mass of a substance to calculate the number of moles in a given mass of that substance and vice versa.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Mole calculations are confined to the two conversions this statement names: mass to amount using the relative formula mass, and amount back to mass. No item requires the molar volume of a gas, the concentration of a solution in mol/dm³, or a calculation of an actual number of particles from the Avogadro constant. The constant is used only for what 4.3.2.1 states about it, that one mole of any substance contains the same number of the stated particles, and the relative formula masses needed are supplied in the stems as AQA supplies them.

concepts.definition: The unit for chemical amount. Chemical amounts are measured in moles, and the symbol for the unit mole is mol. Saying '2 mol of water' states how much water there is as a chemical amount, not as a mass or a volume.

The abbreviation written after a number to show that the number is an amount of substance, for example 0.25 mol. It is never written 'mols' or 'M', and it is not a unit of mass, so a quantity in mol carries no gram value until the relative formula mass is used.

The number obtained by adding together the relative atomic masses of all the atoms shown in the formula of a substance. For CO₂ it is 12 + 16 + 16 = 44. It is a ratio of masses, so it has no unit of its own.

The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass. Mr of CO₂ is 44, so one mole of CO₂ has a mass of 44 g; Ar of carbon is 12, so one mole of carbon atoms has a mass of 12 g.

concepts.term: Equal amounts, equal numbers of particles
concepts.definition: One mole of a substance contains the same number of the stated particles, atoms, molecules or ions as one mole of any other substance. One mole of helium atoms and one mole of uranium atoms contain the same number of atoms, even though their masses in grams are very different.

The number of atoms, molecules or ions in a mole of a given substance. The value of the Avogadro constant is 6.02 x 10²³ per mole. It is a number per mole, not a mass, so it is the same for every substance.

The type of particle a mole is counted in, which must be named before the count means anything. Amounts in moles can apply to atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, formulae and equations, so 'one mole of oxygen' is ambiguous until you say whether the particle is the atom O or the molecule O₂.
amount in moles = mass in grams divided by relative formula mass. 8.0 g of SO₂ (Mr = 64) is 8.0 / 64 = 0.125 mol. Dividing a mass by a mass-like number gives a count, so the answer is in mol.

mass in grams = amount in moles multiplied by relative formula mass. This is the same relationship as amount = mass / Mr with the subject changed. 0.25 mol of MgO (Mr = 40) has a mass of 0.25 x 40 = 10 g.

The masses of reactants and products can be calculated from balanced symbol equations. The equation fixes the ratio in which the substances react, so once one mass is known every other mass in the reaction follows.

Chemical equations can be interpreted in terms of moles: each formula in the equation stands for one mole of that substance, multiplied by its balancing number. The equation is therefore a recipe in amounts, not in masses.

The ratio of the balancing numbers in a balanced symbol equation. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ shows that one mole of magnesium reacts with two moles of hydrochloric acid to produce one mole of magnesium chloride and one mole of hydrogen gas.

The three steps used to get from a given mass to a wanted mass: convert the given mass to an amount in moles using its Mr; use the mole ratio from the balanced equation to find the amount in moles of the wanted substance; convert that amount back to a mass using its Mr.

The balancing numbers in a symbol equation can be calculated from the masses of reactants and products by converting the masses in grams to amounts in moles and converting the numbers of moles to simple whole number ratios.

The smallest set of whole numbers that keeps the amounts in the same proportion. Amounts of 0.25 mol, 0.125 mol and 0.25 mol are in the ratio 2 : 1 : 2, which is the ratio written into the equation; 4 : 2 : 4 has the same proportions but is not the simple whole number ratio.

concepts.term: Changing the subject of an equation
concepts.definition: Rearranging a mathematical relationship so that the quantity you want is on its own. From amount = mass / Mr, multiplying both sides by Mr gives mass = amount x Mr, and dividing both sides into the equation gives Mr = mass / amount.

In a chemical reaction involving two reactants, it is common to use an excess of one of the reactants to ensure that all of the other reactant is used. The reactant in excess is the one that is left over when the reaction stops.

The reactant that is completely used up. It is called the limiting reactant because it limits the amount of products. Which reactant is limiting is decided by comparing amounts in moles against the mole ratio in the balanced equation, not by comparing masses.

The amount of product that can be obtained is fixed by the amount in moles of the limiting reactant and the mole ratio in the equation. Adding more of the reactant that is already in excess cannot increase the amount of product, because there is no more limiting reactant for it to react with.

A measure of how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution. Many chemical reactions take place in solutions, and the concentration of a solution can be measured in mass per given volume of solution.

The unit used here for concentration: the mass of solute in grams that is dissolved in each cubic decimetre of solution. A concentration of 20 g/dm³ means 20 g of solute in every 1 dm³ of solution. Note that 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.

concepts.term: Mass of solute in a given volume
concepts.definition: Because the concentration is a mass per given volume, the mass of solute is found by multiplying the concentration by the volume of solution: mass in g = concentration in g/dm³ x volume in dm³. The volume must be in dm³ before it is used.

concepts.term: How mass and volume set the concentration
concepts.definition: Concentration rises if the mass of solute dissolved rises for the same volume of solution, and falls if the volume of solution rises for the same mass of solute. Doubling the mass of solute doubles the concentration; doubling the volume of solution halves it.

misconceptions.question: A bottle is labelled '2 mol of sodium chloride'. Does this tell you the mass of sodium chloride?
misconceptions.correct: No. It tells you the chemical amount. The mass is only found by multiplying the amount by the relative formula mass of sodium chloride (58.5), giving 117 g.
misconceptions.misconception: A mole is just another word for a gram, so 2 mol means 2 g.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other quantity a student meets in a chemistry lab is weighed out, and moles are always introduced next to masses in grams, so the new unit gets absorbed into the familiar one. Writing 'Mr of CO₂ = 44, so one mole = 44 g' also invites the reading that mol and g are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: Amounts and masses are different quantities with different units. The mole counts particles; the gram measures mass. The relative formula mass is the bridge between them, and it is different for every substance.

misconceptions.question: Do one mole of carbon and one mole of magnesium have the same mass?
misconceptions.correct: No. One mole of carbon has a mass of 12 g and one mole of magnesium has a mass of 24 g, because their relative atomic masses differ. What they share is the number of atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: One mole is a fixed mass, so one mole of anything weighs the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'mole' behaves grammatically like 'kilogram', so students expect it to be a fixed quantity of stuff. The fact that a mole is a fixed number of particles, but not a fixed mass, is a genuinely new idea.
misconceptions.correction: One mole is a fixed number of particles, never a fixed mass. Its mass in grams is numerically equal to the relative formula mass, which changes from substance to substance.

misconceptions.question: One mole of water and one mole of ammonia are compared. Which contains more molecules?
misconceptions.correct: Neither. Both contain the same number of molecules, 6.02 x 10²³, because one mole of a substance contains the same number of the stated particles as one mole of any other substance.
misconceptions.misconception: Water has the larger Mr, so a mole of water must contain more molecules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry over the everyday link between 'more mass' and 'more stuff'. Since a mole of water (18 g) is heavier than a mole of ammonia (17 g), it looks as though there must be more particles in it.
misconceptions.correction: A larger Mr means each individual particle is heavier, not that there are more of them. The count in one mole is fixed at the Avogadro constant for every substance.

misconceptions.question: What sort of quantity is the Avogadro constant?
misconceptions.correct: It is a number of particles per mole: 6.02 x 10²³ per mole. It is a count, not a mass.
misconceptions.misconception: The Avogadro constant is a mass, so 6.02 x 10²³ g is the mass of one mole.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The constant is met in the same lesson as 'mass of one mole', and both are attached to the word mole, so the two get merged. The absence of a familiar unit on 6.02 x 10²³ makes students supply the unit they have just been using.
misconceptions.correction: Read the unit the specification gives: per mole. It answers 'how many particles', not 'how many grams'. The mass of one mole is set by the relative formula mass instead.

misconceptions.question: Is the Avogadro constant 6.02 x 10²³ per gram?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is 6.02 x 10²³ per mole.
misconceptions.misconception: The Avogadro constant is the number of particles in one gram of a substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Grams are the unit students actually handle, so 'per gram' feels like the practical version. Because a mole of carbon happens to be 12 g, some students remember the number as being tied to mass in some way.
misconceptions.correction: The constant is defined per mole. The number of particles in one gram is different for every substance, which is exactly why the mole is needed as a separate unit.

misconceptions.question: One mole of carbon (C) and one mole of carbon dioxide (CO₂) are compared. How do the numbers of particles compare?
misconceptions.correct: One mole of carbon contains the same number of atoms as the number of molecules in one mole of carbon dioxide. Both counts are 6.02 x 10²³.
misconceptions.misconception: A CO₂ molecule has three atoms in it, so a mole of CO₂ contains three times as many particles as a mole of carbon.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The subscript in the formula is a real count, so students apply it in the wrong place: it counts atoms within one molecule, not molecules within one mole. The specification's own example (C and CO₂) exists precisely because this slip is so common.
misconceptions.correction: State the particle first. One mole of CO₂ contains one mole of molecules, the same number as one mole of C atoms. It does contain three moles of atoms, but that is a different stated particle.

misconceptions.question: Can amounts in moles be used for ions and electrons?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The measurement of amounts in moles can apply to atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, formulae and equations.
misconceptions.misconception: Moles only count atoms, because the periodic table is a table of atoms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The mole is introduced through relative atomic mass and the periodic table, so it becomes attached to atoms alone. Ions and electrons are met in a different topic, which keeps them separate in the student's mind.
misconceptions.correction: The mole counts any stated particle. What changes is which particle you name, not whether the mole applies. One mole of Cl⁻ ions and one mole of electrons are both perfectly ordinary amounts.

misconceptions.question: How do you find the amount in moles in 8.0 g of SO₂ (Mr = 64)?
misconceptions.correct: Divide the mass by the relative formula mass: 8.0 / 64 = 0.125 mol.
misconceptions.misconception: You multiply the mass by the relative formula mass, so the answer is 8.0 x 64 = 512 mol.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that mass and Mr are the two numbers involved but not which operation joins them, and multiplying is the first thing tried. A large answer does not look obviously wrong because 6.02 x 10²³ has taught them that mole work involves big numbers.
misconceptions.correction: Check the size of the answer against the mass of one mole. One mole of SO₂ is 64 g, and 8.0 g is much less than that, so the amount must be well below 1 mol. Only dividing gives that.

misconceptions.question: Which number do you divide by to find the moles in 8.0 g of SO₂?
misconceptions.correct: The relative formula mass of the whole substance, 64, not the relative atomic mass of one element in it.
misconceptions.misconception: You use the Ar of the main element, so for SO₂ you divide by 32.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Compound formulae are read as 'sulfur, with some oxygen attached', so the sulfur is treated as the substance and the oxygens as decoration. Students who are shaky on adding up an Mr also fall back on the single number they can find in the periodic table.
misconceptions.correction: Every atom in the formula contributes. SO₂ is 32 + 16 + 16 = 64. The relative formula mass belongs to the substance as a whole.

misconceptions.question: In Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, what does the 2 in front of HCl mean?
misconceptions.correct: Two moles of hydrochloric acid react with each mole of magnesium.
misconceptions.misconception: The 2 means two grams of HCl, so the equation is telling you masses.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing numbers are learned before moles are introduced, so they are first understood as simply 'how many of these you need'. Once masses enter the topic, the nearest available meaning for a number in an equation is a mass.
misconceptions.correction: The balancing numbers give amounts in moles, never masses. To turn them into masses each amount must be multiplied by that substance's own relative formula mass, which differs from substance to substance.

misconceptions.question: In H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, do one mole of H₂ and one mole of Cl₂ have the same mass?
misconceptions.correct: No. One mole of H₂ is 2 g and one mole of Cl₂ is 71 g, even though they react in a 1 : 1 mole ratio.
misconceptions.misconception: If two substances react in a 1 : 1 ratio they must have equal masses.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation looks symmetrical, and 'one to one' is heard as 'the same amount of stuff'. The mole ratio and the mass ratio get treated as the same statement.
misconceptions.correction: Equal amounts in moles mean equal numbers of particles, not equal masses. Each amount has to be multiplied by its own Mr before masses can be compared.

misconceptions.question: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What mass of CaCO₃ gives 28 g of CaO?
misconceptions.correct: 50 g. 28 g of CaO is 28 / 56 = 0.50 mol, the ratio is 1 : 1, so 0.50 mol of CaCO₃ is needed, which is 0.50 x 100 = 50 g.
misconceptions.misconception: The masses on each side must match up substance by substance, so 28 g of CaO must have come from 28 g of CaCO₃.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is taught as 'mass is not lost', which students compress into 'the mass stays the same'. It does hold for the whole reaction mixture, but not for one substance compared with another.
misconceptions.correction: Conservation of mass applies to the total mass of all reactants and all products, not to individual substances. Here 50 g of CaCO₃ gives 28 g of CaO plus 22 g of CO₂, and 28 + 22 = 50.

misconceptions.question: Going from 28 g of CaO to the mass of CaCO₃, do you multiply by 56/100 or by 100/56?
misconceptions.correct: By 100/56, because the substance you want (Mr = 100) is the one whose Mr must end up on the top.
misconceptions.misconception: You just multiply by the two relative formula masses in the order they appear, so 28 x 56 / 100.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ratio shortcuts are memorised without the mole step in between, so the fraction is written down from the order of the numbers on the page rather than from what each number does.
misconceptions.correction: Do the calculation in the three separate steps instead of as one fraction: mass to moles (28 / 56 = 0.50 mol), mole ratio (1 : 1), moles to mass (0.50 x 100 = 50 g). The correct fraction then builds itself.

misconceptions.question: You are given the masses of every reactant and product. How do you find the balancing numbers?
misconceptions.correct: Convert every mass in grams to an amount in moles first, then convert those amounts to a simple whole number ratio.
misconceptions.misconception: You can put the masses straight into a ratio, so 6.0 g : 4.0 g : 10.0 g becomes 3 : 2 : 5.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ratio work in maths is done on the numbers as given, and nothing on the page signals that grams of one substance are not comparable with grams of another. The masses are the numbers in front of the student, so they get used directly.
misconceptions.correction: Grams of different substances count different numbers of particles, so mass ratios are meaningless in an equation. Dividing each mass by its own Mr puts every substance onto the same counting scale first.

misconceptions.question: Amounts of 0.25 mol Mg, 0.125 mol O₂ and 0.25 mol MgO are found. What are the balancing numbers?
misconceptions.correct: 2, 1 and 2, giving 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. The amounts are divided by the smallest, 0.125, to reach the simple whole number ratio.
misconceptions.misconception: Any set of whole numbers in the right proportion will do, so 4Mg + 2O₂ → 4MgO is equally correct.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation does balance, and students are told that balancing means equal atoms on each side, so a scaled-up version passes their own check. The requirement for the simple whole number ratio is an extra condition they have not registered.
misconceptions.correction: The specification asks for simple whole number ratios. Divide every amount by the smallest one and, if the results are not whole, scale up by the smallest factor that makes them whole.

misconceptions.question: From amount = mass / Mr, what is mass equal to?
misconceptions.correct: mass = amount x Mr. Both sides of the relationship are multiplied by Mr.
misconceptions.misconception: You swap the two things that are not wanted, so mass = Mr / amount.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Triangle mnemonics are copied without being understood, and 'move it across and it flips' is remembered as a rule about individual symbols rather than about whole sides of an equation.
misconceptions.correction: Do the algebra on both sides. amount = mass / Mr; multiply both sides by Mr; Mr cancels on the right, leaving amount x Mr = mass. Then test it: 0.25 mol of MgO should give 10 g, and 0.25 x 40 does.

misconceptions.question: 0.10 mol of Mg is added to 0.10 mol of HCl. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Which is the limiting reactant?
misconceptions.correct: The hydrochloric acid. Two moles of HCl are needed for each mole of Mg, so 0.10 mol of Mg would need 0.20 mol of HCl, and only 0.10 mol is present.
misconceptions.misconception: The limiting reactant is simply whichever reactant there is least of, so with equal amounts neither is limiting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Limiting' is glossed as 'the one you run out of', which sounds like a straight comparison of quantities. The mole ratio is left out because in the simplest textbook examples it happens to be 1 : 1.
misconceptions.correction: Compare each amount against what the equation demands, not against the other reactant. Divide each amount by its balancing number: Mg gives 0.10 / 1 = 0.10, HCl gives 0.10 / 2 = 0.05. The smaller result identifies the limiting reactant.

misconceptions.question: In a reaction where the acid is in excess, which reactant limits the amount of product?
misconceptions.correct: The other reactant, the one that is completely used up.
misconceptions.misconception: The reactant in excess is the limiting one, because there is more of it taking part.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'limiting' is heard as 'the big one that sets the size of the reaction', and 'excess' sounds important. The definition is memorised as a label attached to a reactant rather than to the reactant that runs out.
misconceptions.correction: The limiting reactant is the one that is completely used up. The reactant in excess is left over at the end, so it cannot be controlling anything.

misconceptions.question: Zinc is in excess and all the acid has reacted. More zinc is added. Does more hydrogen form?
misconceptions.correct: No. The amount of hydrogen is fixed by the acid, which has already been completely used up.
misconceptions.misconception: Adding more of any reactant always makes more product.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday cooking and in earlier science, adding more ingredients does give more. Reactions are also often pictured as continuing for as long as anything is present, so the idea of one reactant being exhausted is easy to overlook.
misconceptions.correction: Product forms only while both reactants are available. Once the limiting reactant is used up the reaction stops, so extra excess reactant simply sits there unreacted.

misconceptions.question: Two solutions contain the same mass of solute but one has twice the volume. Are they equally concentrated?
misconceptions.correct: No. The one with twice the volume has half the concentration, because the same mass is spread through twice as much solution.
misconceptions.misconception: Concentration depends only on how much solute there is, so equal masses of solute give equal concentrations.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Concentrated' is used in everyday speech as a property of the substance itself, and the mass of solute is the number students actually weighed out, so it feels like the whole story. The volume is treated as a container rather than as part of the measurement.
misconceptions.correction: Concentration is a mass per given volume, so both numbers matter. Divide the mass by the volume in each case: the same mass in a larger volume always gives a smaller concentration.

misconceptions.question: Water is added to a salt solution. What happens to the concentration?
misconceptions.correct: It decreases, because the same mass of solute is now dissolved in a larger volume of solution.
misconceptions.misconception: Adding water increases the concentration, because there is more solution than before.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'More' is read as 'more concentrated' without asking more of what. Adding something to the beaker feels like adding, and the fact that the added substance is the solvent rather than the solute is skipped over.
misconceptions.correction: Adding water adds volume, not solute. The mass of solute stays the same while the volume rises, so the mass per given volume falls. This is what dilution means.

misconceptions.question: What mass of solute is in 250 cm³ of a solution of concentration 8.0 g/dm³?
misconceptions.correct: 2.0 g. First convert the volume: 250 cm³ = 0.250 dm³. Then 8.0 x 0.250 = 2.0 g.
misconceptions.misconception: The volume in cm³ can be put straight into the calculation, giving 8.0 x 250 = 2000 g.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number 250 is the one printed in the question, and the unit mismatch is invisible unless the units are written into the working. Students who do notice often cannot recall whether to multiply or divide by 1000.
misconceptions.correction: The unit g/dm³ requires a volume in dm³. Since 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, divide a volume in cm³ by 1000. A 2000 g answer from a quarter of a litre of solution should also fail any sanity check.

misconceptions.question: How do you find the mass of solute in 0.50 dm³ of a 20 g/dm³ solution?
misconceptions.correct: Multiply: 20 x 0.50 = 10 g.
misconceptions.misconception: You divide the concentration by the volume, giving 20 / 0.50 = 40 g.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Division is associated with the word 'per' in the unit, so students divide somewhere without checking which way round. A larger answer also seems to fit the idea that a solution 'contains a lot'.
misconceptions.correction: Read the unit as a rate: 20 g in every 1 dm³. Half a cubic decimetre must therefore hold half of 20 g. Multiplying the rate by the volume is what a rate always requires.

misconceptions.question: How many moles of chloride ions are in one mole of magnesium chloride, MgCl₂?
misconceptions.correct: Two moles of chloride ions, because each formula unit contains two chloride ions.
misconceptions.misconception: One mole of MgCl₂ contains one mole of chloride ions, because it is one mole of the substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The amount of the compound is transferred unchanged to every particle inside it. The subscript is read as part of the name rather than as a count that scales the amount of that ion.
misconceptions.correction: Name the particle before counting it. One mole of MgCl₂ is one mole of formula units, which is one mole of Mg²⁺ ions and two moles of Cl⁻ ions.

misconceptions.question: 10 g of helium (Ar = 4) and 10 g of neon (Ar = 20) are compared. Which contains more atoms?
misconceptions.correct: The helium. 10 g of helium is 2.5 mol while 10 g of neon is 0.50 mol, so the helium contains five times as many atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Equal masses of two substances contain equal numbers of atoms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Weighing is how students meet quantities of substance, so the balance reading is taken as a measure of how much stuff is present. Without converting to moles there is nothing on the page to say otherwise.
misconceptions.correction: Equal numbers of atoms come from equal amounts in moles, not from equal masses. Convert each mass to moles using its own Ar before comparing.

misconceptions.question: In what unit is the concentration of a solution measured here?
misconceptions.correct: In mass per given volume of solution, for example grams per dm³ (g/dm³).
misconceptions.misconception: Concentration is measured in grams, because it tells you how much solute there is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number students weigh out is a mass in grams, and concentration is introduced immediately afterwards, so the unit that is already in hand gets reused. A single unit also feels simpler than a compound one.
misconceptions.correction: Concentration is a comparison of two quantities, so its unit is a compound one: a mass divided by a volume. Grams alone would not say how much solution the solute is spread through.

misconceptions.question: Is dm³/g the same as g/dm³?
misconceptions.correct: No. g/dm³ is a mass of solute per unit volume of solution; dm³/g would be a volume per unit mass, which is not the concentration.
misconceptions.misconception: It does not matter which way round the two units are written.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Compound units are often copied as a pair of symbols rather than read as a division, so the order looks like a matter of style. In speech 'grams and decimetres cubed' hides the difference entirely.
misconceptions.correction: Read the slash as 'per' and say the unit out loud: grams per cubic decimetre. Turning it over would change the quantity being measured, just as m/s and s/m are different quantities.

misconceptions.question: When measuring the concentration of a solution, which volume is used?
misconceptions.correct: The volume of the solution, not the volume of solvent that was added to make it.
misconceptions.misconception: You use the volume of water you poured in, because that is what you measured.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In practical work the water is measured out and the solid is stirred into it, so the measured volume is the one students remember. The small volume change on dissolving is invisible, which makes the two look identical.
misconceptions.correction: The specification defines concentration as mass per given volume of solution. Solutions are made up to a marked final volume for exactly this reason.

misconceptions.question: One mole of carbon is compared with samples of carbon dioxide. Which sample has the same number of molecules?
misconceptions.correct: One mole of carbon dioxide, because one mole of any substance contains the same number of the stated particles.
misconceptions.misconception: The 12 next to carbon in the periodic table tells you the amount, so you need twelve moles of carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Relative atomic mass and amount are both numbers attached to an element, and if the difference between them has not settled, the number on the periodic table is the one most readily available.
misconceptions.correction: The relative atomic mass sets the mass of one mole in grams; it never sets the amount. The amount is whatever the question states.

misconceptions.question: Is the Avogadro constant 6.02 x 10⁻²³ per mole?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is 6.02 x 10²³ per mole, a very large number.
misconceptions.misconception: The index must be negative because atoms are extremely small.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Standard form with negative indices is used constantly for particle sizes and masses, so the minus sign gets attached to anything to do with atoms. Students copy the pattern rather than asking what is being counted.
misconceptions.correction: The constant counts particles, and there are a huge number of them in a mole, so the index is positive. A negative index would make the count far smaller than one particle.

misconceptions.question: The Mr of CO₂ is 44. What is the mass of one mole of CO₂?
misconceptions.correct: 44 g. The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass.
misconceptions.misconception: There are three atoms in the formula, so you multiply, giving 88 g or 132 g.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The atoms in the formula have already been counted once when the Mr was worked out, but that step is done quickly and then forgotten, so the count gets applied a second time.
misconceptions.correction: The relative formula mass already includes every atom in the formula. Once Mr is found, no further multiplication is needed to get the mass of one mole.

misconceptions.question: In 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, what mass is one mole of the oxygen shown?
misconceptions.correct: 32 g, because the oxygen in the equation is the molecule O₂ and its Mr is 16 + 16 = 32.
misconceptions.misconception: Oxygen is 16, so one mole of the oxygen in the equation is 16 g.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The periodic table gives 16 for oxygen, and that number is reached for automatically. The subscript 2 in O₂ is treated as part of the name of the gas rather than as something that changes the formula mass.
misconceptions.correction: Use the species the equation actually shows. Elements that exist as diatomic molecules, such as O₂, H₂ and Cl₂, have a relative formula mass of twice the relative atomic mass.

misconceptions.question: In Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, how much hydrogen comes from 0.20 mol of magnesium?
misconceptions.correct: 0.20 mol of hydrogen, because the mole ratio of Mg to H₂ is 1 : 1.
misconceptions.misconception: There is a 2 in the equation, so everything in the reaction is doubled, giving 0.40 mol.
misconceptions.whyItArises: One balancing number is taken as a scale factor for the whole equation instead of applying only to the substance it sits in front of. The 2 is the most eye-catching number present, so it gets used everywhere.
misconceptions.correction: Each balancing number belongs to the formula immediately after it. Read the ratio between the two substances you actually care about: here Mg and H₂ both have an implied 1.

misconceptions.question: A solution has a concentration of 20 g/dm³. How much solute is in 0.50 dm³?
misconceptions.correct: 10 g, found by multiplying the concentration by the volume.
misconceptions.misconception: The concentration number is the mass, so any sample of that solution contains 20 g.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number 20 sits next to a gram symbol in the unit, so it is read as a mass of solute already present rather than as a mass for each cubic decimetre. The volume then seems to be extra information.
misconceptions.correction: The unit g/dm³ states a mass for every one cubic decimetre. Only a sample of exactly 1 dm³ contains 20 g; a smaller volume contains proportionately less.

mcqs.stem: A bottle in a laboratory is labelled '0.50 mol of sodium chloride'. What does the '0.50 mol' tell you?

options.text: the chemical amount of sodium chloride present
options.rationale: Chemical amounts are measured in moles, and mol is the symbol for that unit, so the label states an amount of substance.

options.text: the mass of the sodium chloride in grams
options.rationale: Students who treat the mole as another word for the gram read the number as a mass on a balance.

options.text: the number of sodium atoms in the sample
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the mole only ever counts atoms, so the label must be an atom count.

options.text: the volume the sodium chloride takes up
options.rationale: Bottles are usually labelled with volumes, so the unit is assumed to be a measure of space.

mcqs.stem: The relative formula mass of carbon dioxide (CO₂) is 44. What is the mass of one mole of carbon dioxide?

options.rationale: Comes from multiplying the Mr again by a count of atoms that has already been included in working out the Mr.
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass, which is 44.
The Ar of carbon alone is used, ignoring the two oxygen atoms in the formula.
Only the two oxygen atoms are added up, leaving the carbon out of the formula mass.

mcqs.stem: One mole of water (H₂O, Mr = 18) is compared with one mole of ammonia (NH₃, Mr = 17). Which statement is correct?

options.text: Water has more molecules because its Mr is larger.
options.rationale: A larger relative formula mass is read as meaning more particles rather than heavier particles.

options.text: Ammonia has more molecules because it has more atoms.
options.rationale: The four atoms in NH₃ are used to scale up the number of molecules, applying the formula in the wrong place.

options.text: They contain exactly the same number of molecules.
options.rationale: One mole of a substance contains the same number of the stated particles as one mole of any other substance.

options.text: They have the same mass because both are one mole.
options.rationale: Picked by students who believe one mole is a fixed mass rather than a fixed number of particles.

mcqs.stem: What is the value of the Avogadro constant?

options.rationale: The familiar unit of mass is substituted for the mole, which would make the constant differ for every substance.
The negative index is copied from the standard form used for the sizes and masses of particles.
The constant is treated as a mass, merging it with the idea of the mass of one mole.
This is the number of atoms, molecules or ions in a mole of a given substance, exactly as the specification states it.

mcqs.stem: One mole of carbon (C) contains a certain number of atoms. Which sample contains that same number of molecules?

options.text: one mole of carbon dioxide, CO₂
options.rationale: The specification gives this example directly: one mole of any substance contains the same number of the stated particles.

options.text: three moles of carbon dioxide, CO₂
options.rationale: The three atoms in a CO₂ molecule are used to scale the amount up, confusing atoms within a molecule with molecules within a mole.

options.text: one third of a mole of carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think a mole of the heavier CO₂ already holds more particles, so less than a mole is needed.

options.text: twelve moles of carbon dioxide, CO₂
options.rationale: The relative atomic mass of carbon is read off the periodic table and used as though it were an amount in moles.

mcqs.stem: What is the amount, in moles, in 8.0 g of sulfur dioxide (SO₂, Mr = 64)?

options.rationale: The mass is multiplied by the relative formula mass instead of divided by it.
amount = mass / Mr = 8.0 / 64 = 0.125 mol, which is sensible because 8.0 g is much less than the 64 g in one mole.
The mass in grams is quoted straight back as an amount, treating mol and g as interchangeable.
Only the Ar of sulfur, 32, is used as the divisor, leaving the two oxygen atoms out.

mcqs.stem: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of magnesium oxide (MgO, Mr = 40)?

options.rationale: The rearrangement is done by flipping symbols, giving Mr divided by amount rather than Mr multiplied by amount.
Follows from believing amount = mass x Mr, which turns the mass calculation into a division.
mass = amount x Mr = 0.25 x 40 = 10 g, a quarter of the 40 g in one mole.
The mass of one mole is given, with the 0.25 mol left out of the calculation altogether.

mcqs.stem: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. What mass of magnesium oxide is formed when 48 g of magnesium burns completely? (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)

options.rationale: Conservation of mass is applied substance by substance, so the product is assumed to weigh the same as the magnesium.
The oxygen is taken as single atoms of mass 16 rather than as O₂ molecules of mass 32, so 48 + 16 is used.
The balancing number 2 is applied a second time, doubling a result that already includes it.
48 g of Mg is 48 / 24 = 2.0 mol; the ratio Mg : MgO is 2 : 2, so 2.0 mol of MgO forms, and 2.0 x 40 = 80 g.

mcqs.stem: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. What mass of calcium carbonate is needed to make 28 g of calcium oxide? (Mr: CaCO₃ = 100, CaO = 56, CO₂ = 44)

options.rationale: 28 g of CaO is 28 / 56 = 0.50 mol; the ratio is 1 : 1, so 0.50 mol of CaCO₃ is needed, and 0.50 x 100 = 50 g.
The mass is carried across unchanged, treating conservation of mass as applying to each substance separately.
The ratio of the two formula masses is used upside down, multiplying by 56/100 instead of 100/56.
The mass of one mole of CaCO₃ is given, without scaling for the 0.50 mol actually required.

mcqs.stem: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What amount of hydrogen is produced when 0.20 mol of magnesium reacts completely with an excess of hydrochloric acid?

options.rationale: The 2 in front of HCl is applied to the whole equation, doubling the hydrogen as well.
The equation shows one mole of magnesium producing one mole of hydrogen, so the amounts are equal.
The amount is halved because hydrogen is diatomic, treating the subscript as though it changed the mole ratio.
The balancing number 2 is read off as the answer, ignoring the 0.20 mol given in the question.

mcqs.stem: In the equation Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, what does the 2 in front of HCl tell you?

options.text: Two grams of HCl react with one gram of Mg.
options.rationale: The balancing numbers are read as masses in grams, which is the unit students are most used to.

options.text: Two moles of every substance shown are needed.
options.rationale: One balancing number is treated as a scale factor for the whole equation rather than for HCl alone.

options.text: Two moles of HCl react with one mole of Mg.
options.rationale: Chemical equations can be interpreted in terms of moles, and each balancing number gives the amount of that substance.

options.text: Each HCl molecule contains two hydrogen atoms.
options.rationale: The balancing number is confused with a subscript inside the formula.

mcqs.stem: 6.0 g of magnesium reacts with 4.0 g of oxygen to form 10.0 g of magnesium oxide. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16.) Which balanced equation fits these masses?

options.rationale: The masses 6.0 : 4.0 : 10.0 are put straight into a ratio without converting to moles.
The amount of oxygen is worked out from Ar = 16 instead of the O₂ formula mass of 32, giving a 1 : 1 : 1 ratio that does not balance.
The proportions are right but they have not been reduced to the simple whole number ratio.
The amounts are 6.0/24 = 0.25 mol Mg, 4.0/32 = 0.125 mol O₂ and 10.0/40 = 0.25 mol MgO, a ratio of 2 : 1 : 2.

mcqs.stem: You are given the mass of every reactant and product and asked to find the balancing numbers for the equation. What must you do first?

options.text: Convert each mass in grams into an amount in moles.
options.rationale: The specification's method converts the masses in grams to amounts in moles before any ratio is taken.

options.text: Write the masses in grams as a simple whole ratio.
options.rationale: The masses are treated as directly comparable, which they are not because each substance has a different Mr.

options.text: Divide every mass by the smallest mass that is given.
options.rationale: The dividing step is remembered but applied to masses instead of to the amounts in moles.

options.text: Add the reactant masses and compare with the products.
options.rationale: A conservation of mass check is done, which is useful but gives no balancing numbers.

mcqs.stem: The relationship between amount, mass and relative formula mass is: amount in moles = mass / Mr. Which rearrangement of it is correct?

options.rationale: The two symbols are swapped over rather than the same operation being done to both sides.

options.text: mass = amount in moles x Mr
options.rationale: Multiplying both sides by Mr cancels it on the right and leaves mass on its own.

options.text: Mr = amount in moles x mass
options.rationale: Follows from mis-remembering the original relationship as a multiplication.
The original relationship is written upside down, so the units no longer make sense.

mcqs.stem: Two reactants are mixed and one of them is added in excess. Which reactant is the limiting reactant?

options.text: the reactant that is added in excess
options.rationale: The word excess is taken to mean the reactant in control of the reaction.

options.text: the reactant with the smaller mass used
options.rationale: Masses are compared directly, without using the mole ratio from the equation.

options.text: the reactant that is completely used up
options.rationale: The specification defines the limiting reactant as the reactant that is completely used up, because it limits the amount of products.

options.text: the reactant with the larger formula mass
options.rationale: A number from the periodic table is used in place of the amounts actually present.

mcqs.stem: Why is one reactant often used in excess in a chemical reaction?

options.text: to make more product than the equation allows
options.rationale: Adding more reactant is assumed always to give more product, whatever the equation says.

options.text: to make the excess reactant the limiting one
options.rationale: The labels are swapped, so excess is treated as a way of putting a reactant in control.

options.text: to make sure both reactants run out together
options.rationale: Excess is confused with using exactly the amounts the equation requires.

options.text: to make sure all of the other reactant is used
options.rationale: This is the reason the specification gives: an excess of one reactant ensures the other is completely used up.

mcqs.stem: 0.10 mol of magnesium is added to 0.10 mol of hydrochloric acid. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. What amount of hydrogen is produced?

options.rationale: The acid is limiting: 0.10 mol of HCl needs only 0.05 mol of Mg, and the HCl : H₂ ratio of 2 : 1 gives 0.05 mol of hydrogen.
The two amounts are compared directly, so with equal amounts the magnesium is assumed to react fully in a 1 : 1 ratio.
The balancing number 2 is applied to the product instead of to the hydrochloric acid.
The amount is halved twice, dividing by the balancing number a second time.

mcqs.stem: Zinc is added to hydrochloric acid. All of the acid reacts and some zinc is left over. What happens to the mass of hydrogen made if more zinc is added to the same acid?

options.text: It increases, as there is now more zinc to react.
options.rationale: More reactant is assumed always to give more product, regardless of which reactant has run out.

options.text: It stays the same, as the acid is the limiting one.
options.rationale: The acid was completely used up, so it limits the amount of product; extra zinc has nothing left to react with.

options.text: It increases, as zinc must be the limiting one.
options.rationale: The reactant in excess is mislabelled as limiting, so adding it seems to raise the yield.

options.text: It stays the same, as the zinc has all been used.
options.rationale: Contradicted by the question, which says some zinc is left over, so the zinc cannot have run out.

mcqs.stem: Which of these could be a unit for the concentration of a solution?

options.rationale: The compound unit is copied with the two parts the wrong way round, which measures a different quantity.
Concentration is treated as a mass, because a mass in grams is what gets weighed out.
Concentration can be measured in mass per given volume of solution, for example grams per dm³ (g/dm³).
The volume alone is quoted, which describes how much solution there is but not how concentrated it is.

mcqs.stem: A solution has a concentration of 20 g/dm³. What mass of solute is present in 0.50 dm³ of this solution?

options.rationale: The concentration is divided by the volume instead of multiplied by it.
The concentration number is read as the mass of solute in any sample, so the volume is ignored.
The volume is divided by the concentration, which inverts the calculation.
The unit means 20 g in every 1 dm³, so 0.50 dm³ contains 20 x 0.50 = 10 g.

mcqs.stem: What mass of solute is present in 250 cm³ of a solution with a concentration of 8.0 g/dm³?

options.rationale: The volume in cm³ is used without converting to dm³, so the answer is 1000 times too large.
The concentration is divided by the volume rather than multiplied by it.
The conversion is done the wrong way, multiplying by 4 instead of dividing by 4.

mcqs.stem: Water is added to a solution of sodium chloride. The mass of dissolved sodium chloride does not change. What happens to the concentration of the solution?

options.text: It rises, as there is now more solution present.
options.rationale: Adding anything to the beaker is read as making the solution more concentrated.

options.text: It falls, as the same mass is in a larger volume.
options.rationale: Concentration is a mass per given volume, so raising the volume while the mass stays fixed lowers it.

options.text: It stays the same, as the solute mass is the same.
options.rationale: Concentration is treated as depending on the mass of solute alone, with volume ignored.

options.text: It falls, as some of the solute leaves the solution.
options.rationale: The right direction reached by false reasoning: no solute is removed from the solution when water is added.

mcqs.stem: Solution A and solution B contain the same mass of dissolved solute. Solution A has twice the volume of solution B. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A is twice as concentrated as B.
options.rationale: More solution is read as more concentrated, so the volume is applied the wrong way round.

options.text: A and B have equal concentrations.
options.rationale: Equal masses of solute are taken to mean equal concentrations, ignoring the volumes.

options.text: A is half as concentrated as B.
options.rationale: The same mass spread through twice the volume gives half the mass per given volume.

options.text: A is four times more dilute than B.
options.rationale: The factor of two is applied twice over, as though it affected mass and volume.

mcqs.stem: One mole of magnesium chloride, MgCl₂, is dissolved in water. What amount of chloride ions does this produce?

options.rationale: The amount of the compound is transferred unchanged to the ion inside it.
All three atoms shown in the formula are counted, rather than the chloride ions alone.
The amount is divided by the subscript instead of multiplied by it.
Each MgCl₂ formula unit contains two chloride ions, so one mole of the compound gives two moles of Cl⁻ ions.

mcqs.stem: A 10 g sample of helium (Ar = 4) is compared with a 10 g sample of neon (Ar = 20). Which sample contains more atoms?

options.text: helium, because 10 g is more moles of helium
options.rationale: 10 g of helium is 2.5 mol while 10 g of neon is 0.50 mol, and more moles means more atoms.

options.text: neither, because the two masses are the same
options.rationale: Equal masses are assumed to hold equal numbers of atoms, which is only true for equal amounts.

options.text: neon, because each neon atom is much heavier
options.rationale: A heavier particle is taken to mean a greater number of particles.

options.text: neon, because its atoms take up more space
options.rationale: Atomic size is used in place of the amount in moles.

mcqs.stem: The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to which quantity?

options.text: the number of atoms in its formula
options.rationale: The atom count in the formula is used again, although it was already included when Mr was worked out.
This is the relationship the specification states, so a substance with Mr = 44 has 44 g in one mole.
The constant is treated as a mass rather than as a number of particles per mole.

options.text: the number of protons in one atom
options.rationale: The atomic number is used in place of the relative formula mass.

mcqs.stem: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. (Ar: H = 1, O = 16.) Which set of masses does this equation show?

options.text: 2 g H₂ + 32 g O₂ → 34 g H₂O
options.rationale: The balancing number 2 is not applied to the hydrogen, so only one mole of H₂ is costed.

options.text: 4 g H₂ + 16 g O₂ → 20 g H₂O
options.rationale: Oxygen is taken as single atoms of mass 16 rather than as O₂ molecules of mass 32.

options.text: 4 g H₂ + 32 g O₂ → 36 g H₂O
options.rationale: Two moles of H₂ is 2 x 2 = 4 g, one mole of O₂ is 32 g and two moles of H₂O is 2 x 18 = 36 g, and 4 + 32 = 36.

options.text: 2 g H₂ + 2 g O₂ → 4 g H₂O
options.rationale: Substances in the equation are assumed to react in equal masses because the amounts look comparable.
